headline: Neap Tide Slack Turns the New Haven Breakwalls Into a Porgy Clinic
subhead: Light current off the outer wall stacked scup three deep on the same drop, with sea bass mixed in and blackfish starting to test the rocks.
body_markdown:
Thursday morning, outer New Haven breakwall, and I'm standing there with a spinning rod that's basically a toy — 10-pound braid, a size 4 hook, half a green crab pinched on — and I'm hooked up before the anchor's even settled. That's not exaggeration, that's just what a slack current does to a rockpile full of porgies. Three fish deep on the same drop, biggest one nudging 13 inches, and I hadn't even finished my coffee.

We flagged this a few days back — said the neap tide coming in around the 5th and 6th would ease the current on structure and make the bottom bite sharper, and that's exactly what showed up. Less push means your bait sits still instead of getting dragged sideways off the rocks, and for porgies and sea bass that's the difference between a nibble you can't convert and a fish in the cooler. The current's starting to build again now as we move away from neap, but for the first half of this week it was about as clean as bottom fishing gets on this stretch.

The scup bite has been the headline all week — outer breakwall, Charles Island rockpile, and the humps off Falkner Island are all holding fish in the 8-to-15-foot range depending on tide stage. High-low rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, squid strips or clam belly, fished tight to the rock edges on the last of the incoming through the top of the tide. That's when the current lays down enough to actually feel the bite instead of just feeling your sinker bounce.

Sea bass are mixed right in with the porgies on the same drops, which is the pattern you want in August — steady water in the mid-70s keeps them locked onto structure instead of wandering, and they're not picky. Squid strips, clam, even a chunk of porgy from the last fish work fine. I had a stretch off Falkner Island where every third drop was a keeper sea bass, 14 to 16 inches, nothing huge but a nice mixed bag with the scup filling out the rest of the cooler.

Blackfish are the wildcard right now. I'm marking them on the rockpiles — Charles Island, the Gulf rocks off Milford, a few spots along the New Haven wall — but they're not fully committing yet. Green crabs on a jig head, dropped right into the pockets between boulders, got me two teasing bites and one fish that came unbuttoned at the surface. Water's still on the warm side for them to go full aggressive. I'd expect that to sharpen up as we get into September and the temps ease off a touch, but if you want to scout now, half crabs on light tackle in the 10-to-20-foot zone around the rockier structure is the move — just don't expect a banner day yet.

Stripers are the tougher conversation. The Charles Island sandbar has been giving up fish, but it's a nighttime and dawn program right now — daytime action off that bar has gone quiet with the warm water sitting up top. I fished the bar on an outgoing tide right before first light with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig and picked off two schoolies in the 22-to-25-inch range before the sun got high and shut it down. If you want a shot at something better, Stratford Shoal at night on bucktails or swimming a live eel along the edge where the current breaks is still your best bet for a bigger fish — that structure holds bass that don't want to fight bright sun and warm surface water.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — snapper blues thick in the harbor and around Hammonasset, adult blues showing occasionally where bait pods bunch up off the breakwalls. Nothing like a sustained blitz yet, but with peanut bunker starting to spread through the harbor mouths, I wouldn't be shocked if that cocktail blue bite in the back coves sharpens up over the next week or two as those bait schools thicken. Worth keeping a bucktail or a small popper rigged and ready if you're bottom fishing and see bait get nervous on the surface.

Fluke have been the quiet, dependable piece of the puzzle. Drifting the sandy edges off Charles Island and the deeper channel water toward Stratford Shoal with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails has been picking off keeper-class fish in the 18-to-20-inch range, mixed with plenty of shorts you'll have to sort through. Nothing spectacular, but steady enough to fill out a dinner if the tide's right.

Looking ahead — current's rebuilding now off that neap low, which usually means the bottom bite gets a little more technical again. You'll want to fish it smarter: slower drifts, heavier sinkers to hold bottom, and picking the tide stages where the push eases even briefly. If the stable weather holds, I'd put my money on the porgy and sea bass action staying strong through the weekend, with blackfish starting to show real commitment as we roll toward Labor Day. For stripers, I'd keep it a dawn-and-dusk game at Charles Island and save the serious effort for Stratford Shoal after dark.
